CHAPTER 3.3 · LEARNING AREA 3 · MARCH

Systems of linear equations

Pheasants and rabbits sit in a cage, with 35 heads and 94 legs altogether. How many animals of each kind are there? Two unknowns need two equations. You will learn to solve systems of linear equations graphically as two lines and by calculation, when there is exactly one, no or infinitely many solutions and how to model real-life problems with them.

12 LESSONS3 UNITSMODELLINGCAS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • translate real-life problems with two unknowns into a system of equations
  • solve systems of equations graphically: two lines, one point of intersection
  • solve systems of equations by calculation, without aids and with the CAS
  • distinguish all cases of solvability and assess graphical and algebraic methods

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Solving systems of equations graphically

An adult ticket costs $e$ euros, a ticket for young people $j$ euros. The equation $2e + 3j = 39$ has many solutions, for example $e = 12, j = 5$ or $e = 15, j = 3$. All its solutions together form a straight line. The second equation $e + 4j = 32$ is a second line. Only their point of intersection satisfies both equations.

KEY POINT · SOLVING SYSTEMS OF EQUATIONS GRAPHICALLY

A system of linear equations with two equations and two unknowns has the form

$\begin{aligned} \text{I:}&\quad ax + by = c \\ \text{II:}&\quad dx + ey = f \end{aligned}$

A solution is a pair of numbers $(x, y)$ that satisfies both equations.

Graphically: rearrange both equations for $y$, draw the lines, read off the point of intersection and verify it by substituting into both equations.

Modelling in four steps: 1. Define the unknowns, with their meaning. 2. Set up two equations. 3. Solve. 4. Check against the situation and answer.

Reading off has its limits: if the point of intersection is at $(2.35, 2.85)$, you cannot read it off exactly.

INTERACTIVE · TWO EQUATIONS, TWO LINES

Change $a$, $b$ and $c$ in equation II and watch the point of intersection. Can you find settings without a point of intersection?

EXAMPLE 1 · READING OFF

Solve graphically: I: $y = -x + 5$, II: $y = 0.5x + 2$.

The lines intersect at $S(2, 3)$, as in the picture at the start of the chapter.

Check: I: $-2 + 5 = 3$, II: $1 + 2 = 3$. So $L = \{(2, 3)\}$.

EXAMPLE 2 · CINEMA TICKETS

Solve the cinema problem from the explorations graphically.

With $j$ horizontal and $e$ vertical: I: $e = 19.5 - 1.5j$, II: $e = 32 - 4j$. The lines intersect at $j = 5$, $e = 12$.

Adults pay €12, young people €5. Check: $24 + 15 = 39$ and $12 + 20 = 32$.

EXERCISES

Solve graphically and check: a) $y = 2x - 1$, $y = -x + 5$   b) $y = x + 1$, $y = -2x + 4$   c) $x + y = 6$, $x - y = 2$

a) $(2, 3)$   b) $(1, 2)$   c) rearranged for $y$, $y = -x + 6$ and $y = x - 2$: $(4, 2)$

Is $(3, -1)$ a solution of I: $2x + y = 5$, II: $x - 2y = 5$?

I: $6 - 1 = 5$, II: $3 + 2 = 5$. Both are true, so yes.

Contract A costs €10 a month and €0.05 per minute, contract B €4 a month and €0.15 per minute. Set up both costs as equations, draw them and read off when both cost the same.

$k = 10 + 0.05t$ and $k = 4 + 0.15t$. The same at $6 = 0.1t$, so at 60 minutes (€13). If you phone more, A is better for you.

A rectangle has a perimeter of 26 cm. Its length is 3 cm greater than its width. Set up a system of equations and solve it graphically.

$2a + 2b = 26$ and $a = b + 3$. Point of intersection: $b = 5$, $a = 8$. The rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide.

Read off the point of intersection of $y = 0.7x + 1.2$ and $y = -1.3x + 5.9$ as precisely as possible. Why is that difficult? Then calculate it.

Read off: about $(2.4, 2.8)$. Calculated: $2x = 4.7$, $x = 2.35$ and $y = 0.7 \cdot 2.35 + 1.2 = 2.845$. Between the grid lines you can only estimate roughly.

UNIT 2CAS · 4 LESSONS

2Solving systems of equations by calculation

Pheasants $f$ and rabbits $h$: I: $f + h = 35$ (heads), II: $2f + 4h = 94$ (legs). From I it follows that $f = 35 - h$. If you substitute this into II, an equation with only one unknown is left: $2(35 - h) + 4h = 94$, so $70 + 2h = 94$, $h = 12$ and $f = 23$.

All the methods of calculation have the same idea: one unknown is eliminated, and then a linear equation is left that you can already solve. You do not have to master all three methods. Choose one and practise it until you are confident.

KEY POINT · SOLVING BY CALCULATION

Substitution method: rearrange one equation for one unknown and substitute it into the other.

Equating method: rearrange both equations for the same unknown and set them equal.

Elimination method: multiply the equations by numbers so that one unknown disappears when you add them.

Then calculate the second unknown, check in both equations and state the solution set: $L = \{(x, y)\}$.

Which method? If one unknown already stands alone: substitute. If both equations are given as $y = \ldots$: equate. If the numbers in front of one unknown have opposite signs: add.

CAS: with awkward numbers the calculator does the work, for example with solve(1.7x+2.3y=9.1 and 0.4x-1.1y=-2.6,{x,y}).

INTERACTIVE · STEP BY STEP

Choose a method and reveal the steps one by one. Work out each step yourself first. At the end you see the two lines and their point of intersection.

EXAMPLE 3 · SUBSTITUTING

Solve I: $y = 3x - 1$, II: $2x + y = 9$.

I into II: $2x + 3x - 1 = 9$, so $5x = 10$ and $x = 2$. Then $y = 3 \cdot 2 - 1 = 5$.

Check: I: $5 = 6 - 1$, II: $4 + 5 = 9$. $L = \{(2, 5)\}$

EXAMPLE 4 · ADDING

Solve I: $3x + 4y = 22$, II: $5x - 2y = 2$.

II times 2: $10x - 4y = 4$. Added to I: $13x = 26$, so $x = 2$. In I: $6 + 4y = 22$, $y = 4$.

Check in II: $10 - 8 = 2$. $L = \{(2, 4)\}$

EXERCISES

Solve with the substitution method: a) $y = 2x$, $x + y = 12$   b) $x = 4 - y$, $3x + 2y = 10$   c) $y = x + 3$, $2x - y = 1$

a) $3x = 12$: $(4, 8)$   b) $12 - 3y + 2y = 10$, $y = 2$: $(2, 2)$   c) $2x - x - 3 = 1$, $x = 4$: $(4, 7)$

Solve with the equating method: a) $y = 3x - 5$, $y = x + 1$   b) $y = -2x + 7$, $y = 0.5x + 2$

a) $3x - 5 = x + 1$, $x = 3$: $(3, 4)$   b) $-2.5x = -5$, $x = 2$: $(2, 3)$

Solve with the elimination method: a) $x + y = 10$, $x - y = 4$   b) $2x + 3y = 12$, $4x - 3y = 6$   c) $3x + 2y = 7$, $2x + 5y = 12$

For c), multiply I by 2 and II by 3. Then subtract.

a) $2x = 14$: $(7, 3)$   b) $6x = 18$, $x = 3$, $y = 2$: $(3, 2)$   c) $6x + 4y = 14$ and $6x + 15y = 36$, so $11y = 22$, $y = 2$, $x = 1$: $(1, 2)$

In a car park there are cars and motorbikes, 26 vehicles with 84 wheels altogether. How many are there of each kind?

$a + m = 26$ and $4a + 2m = 84$. With $m = 26 - a$: $4a + 52 - 2a = 84$, $a = 16$. So 16 cars and 10 motorbikes.

CAS Solve with the CAS: $1.7x + 2.3y = 9.1$ and $0.4x - 1.1y = -2.6$. Check with the values rounded to two decimal places. What do you notice?

The CAS gives $x = \tfrac{13}{9} \approx 1.44$ and $y = \tfrac{26}{9} \approx 2.89$. With rounded values the check only works roughly: $1.7 \cdot 1.44 + 2.3 \cdot 2.89 = 9.095$. Exact fractions are more precise.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Solvability and modelling

Two lines in the plane can intersect at one point, lie parallel next to each other or lie exactly on top of each other. There are no other possibilities. That is why exactly these three cases also occur for the solutions of a system of equations.

KEY POINT · THREE CASES

The lines intersect: exactly one solution.

The lines are parallel and different: no solution, $L = \{\,\}$. The calculation leads to a contradiction like $0 = 4$.

The lines are identical: infinitely many solutions. The calculation leads to a true statement like $0 = 0$.

Because there are no further cases, this is a complete case distinction.

Graphically or by calculation? The picture shows at once which case it is, but it is imprecise. The calculation is precise, but you see nothing. It is best to use both.

Looking ahead: three unknowns need three equations. Instead of lines in the plane these are planes in space, and you solve them with Gaussian elimination, which you will get to know in Year 11.

INTERACTIVE · HOW DO TWO LINES LIE?

Choose the examples “intersecting”, “parallel” and “identical” and compare the gradients and y-intercepts. “Orthogonal” means perpendicular to each other, a special case of intersecting.

EXAMPLE 5 · NO SOLUTION

Solve I: $2x + y = 3$, II: $4x + 2y = 10$.

I times 2: $4x + 2y = 6$. Subtracted from II: $0 = 4$, a contradiction. $L = \{\,\}$

In the picture: $y = -2x + 3$ and $y = -2x + 5$ have the same gradient and different y-intercepts. They are parallel.

EXAMPLE 6 · TWO CANDLES

A red candle is 24 cm long and burns down 2 cm per hour. A white one is 18 cm long and burns down 1.5 cm per hour. Will they ever be the same length?

$r = 24 - 2t$ and $w = 18 - 1.5t$. The same length: $24 - 2t = 18 - 1.5t$, so $t = 12$ and $r = w = 0$.

They are only the same length after 12 hours, and then both have burnt down. The calculation is right, but the answer has to be checked against the situation.

EXERCISES

Decide without calculating how many solutions there are: a) $y = 2x + 1$, $y = 2x - 3$   b) $y = 2x + 1$, $y = -2x + 1$   c) $y = 2x + 1$, $2y = 4x + 2$

a) none, parallel   b) exactly one, $(0, 1)$   c) infinitely many, both are the same line

Solve by calculation and interpret the result: a) $x + y = 4$, $2x + 2y = 8$   b) $x - y = 1$, $y = x + 2$

a) II is twice I, what is left is $0 = 0$: infinitely many solutions   b) $x - x - 2 = 1$ gives $-2 = 1$: no solution

For which value of $c$ does the system $x + 2y = 5$, $2x + 4y = c$ have infinitely many solutions, for which values none?

For $c = 10$, II is twice I: infinitely many. For every other $c$ the lines are parallel: no solution.

A sports club charges adults €15 and young people €8 a month. It has 120 members and takes €1240 a month. How many adults are members?

$e + j = 120$ and $15e + 8j = 1240$. With $j = 120 - e$: $7e + 960 = 1240$, $e = 40$. So 40 adults and 80 young people.

Assess the advantages and disadvantages of the graphical and the algebraic method. To do so, solve $0.3x + 0.7y = 2.1$ and $1.2x - 0.4y = 0.6$ in both ways.

Calculated: $x = 1.3125$, $y = 2.4375$. Graphically you only read off about $(1.3, 2.4)$. But the picture shows at once that there is exactly one solution, and it is a good check for the calculation.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many solutions does $y = 2x + 1$, $y = 2x - 3$ have?

The same gradient, different intercepts.

For which $c$ are there infinitely many solutions in exercise 13?

$2 \cdot 5$

How many adults does the sports club in exercise 14 have?

$7e = 280$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Solve with a method of your choice: a) $2x + y = 7$, $x - y = 2$   b) $3x - 2y = 4$, $x + 2y = 12$

a) Adding: $3x = 9$, $x = 3$, $y = 1$   b) Adding: $4x = 16$, $x = 4$, $y = 4$

From juice with 90% fruit content and juice with 40% fruit content, 10 litres with 60% fruit content are to be mixed. How much of each kind do you need?

$a + b = 10$ and $0.9a + 0.4b = 6$. With $b = 10 - a$: $0.5a + 4 = 6$, $a = 4$. So 4 l of the 90% juice and 6 l of the 40% juice.

Two numbers have the sum 50 and the difference 14. What are they?

$x + y = 50$ and $x - y = 14$: $2x = 64$, so 32 and 18.

A boat travels 24 km downstream in 2 hours and the same distance upstream in 3 hours. How fast is the boat in still water, how fast does the river flow?

Downstream the speeds of the boat and the river add up, upstream they are subtracted.

$b + f = 12$ and $b - f = 8$ (both in km/h). So $b = 10$ km/h and $f = 2$ km/h.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Pheasants and rabbits in the same cage

The puzzle from the start of the chapter is more than 1500 years old. It appears in the Chinese arithmetic book of Master Sun, the Sunzi suanjing, which was written between the 3rd and the 5th century: “Now there are pheasants and rabbits in the same cage. Above there are 35 heads, below 94 feet.”

Systems of equations were not known at that time. The book solves the problem with a lovely trick: you halve the number of feet and get 47. Now, in your mind, every pheasant stands on one leg and every rabbit on two. If you subtract the 35 heads, exactly one leg is left over for each rabbit: 12 rabbits. The remaining 23 animals are pheasants.

Your system of equations from unit 2 gives the same. The trick only works for exactly this puzzle, the system of equations for all similar ones.

Source: Sunzi suanjing (Master Sun’s Mathematical Manual), volume 3, China, 3rd to 5th century.
